prompt: BRITTLE
explanation: A brittle thing snaps instead of giving way, so "easily broken" is the match. The other three name ways a material yields without breaking: "easily bent" is the one thing a brittle thing cannot do, "easily stretched" belongs to something elastic, and "easily softened" to something that answers to heat or water. All four say how a material behaves under force, and only one of them ends in a break.

prompt: JEER
explanation: To jeer is to call out at someone in scorn, which is what "mock" names. "Cheer" is the same crowd noise turned toward approval instead; "whisper" fixes how loudly a thing is said rather than the attitude behind it; and "warn" tells a person of a danger, which a jeer never troubles to do.

prompt: SUMMON
explanation: To summon someone is to send word that they are to come, so "call for" is the match. "Wait for" leaves the other person to decide whether to appear, which is the opposite of a summons; "pay for" makes the matter a purchase; and "stand for" is to represent something or to put up with it. All four are things one person can do with respect to another, and only one of them brings him to you.

prompt: MEDDLE
explanation: To meddle is to push into a matter that is not yours, which is what "interfere" names. "Mediate" also puts a person into someone else's quarrel, but a mediator has been invited in and works to settle it; "assist" is help that was wanted; and "observe" keeps to watching and touches nothing. All four describe someone near another person's business, and only one of them is unwelcome there.

prompt: QUELL
explanation: To quell a disturbance is to stop it, so "put an end to" is the match. The other three are also things that can be done about a revolt: "give in to" grants its demands, "take part in" joins it, and "spread word of" carries the news of it further. Only one of the four leaves the disturbance over.

prompt: ASTUTE
explanation: An astute person sees quickly what is really going on and what it is worth, which is what "shrewd" names. "Learned" reports a stock of knowledge, and a very learned person may still miss what is in front of him; "honest" reports character rather than perception; and "stubborn" reports an unwillingness to be moved. All four are compliments or complaints one might make about the same person, and only one of them concerns how sharply he reads a situation.

prompt: SCRUTINIZE
explanation: To scrutinize a document is to go over it looking for what it contains, so "examine closely" is the match. "Copy carefully" shares the care but reproduces the page instead of inspecting it; "summarize briefly" cuts it down to its substance; and "set aside quietly" puts off dealing with it at all. All four are things a clerk can do with the same file.

prompt: NOTORIOUS
explanation: A notorious person or place is famous in the wrong direction, so "widely known for something bad" is the match. "Widely admired for skill" keeps the fame and loses the disgrace; "known only to a few" keeps the disgrace available but takes away the reach; and "newly discovered" reports how recently a thing came to light rather than what it is known for.

prompt: INCESSANT
explanation: Something incessant goes on and on without a break, which is what "unceasing" names. "Occasional" comes and goes, "brief" is over quickly, and "sudden" describes how a thing begins rather than how long it goes on. All four describe a pattern a noise can follow, and only one of them never stops.

prompt: DISPARAGE
explanation: To disparage someone's work is to speak of it as worth less than it is, which is what "belittle" names. "Summarize" restates the work without judging it; "recommend" judges it in the opposite direction; and "exaggerate" distorts the scale of a thing, which may flatter it as easily as it may damage it. All four are things a reviewer can do to the same book.

prompt: INEXORABLE
explanation: An inexorable process keeps going whatever is put in its way, so "impossible to stop" is the match. "Impossible to explain" concerns whether it can be understood, "impossible to repeat" whether it can happen twice, and "impossible to afford" what it would cost — a process can be any of those and still be halted tomorrow.

prompt: MAGNANIMOUS
explanation: Magnanimous names the largeness of spirit that lets a winner spare the one he beat, so "forgiving" is the match. "Imposing" is largeness of presence, "wealthy" is largeness of means, and "boastful" is what a victor sounds like when his spirit is small. All four could be said of the same man on the same afternoon, and only one of them concerns how he treats the loser.

prompt: ACRIMONIOUS
explanation: An acrimonious dispute is carried on with real ill feeling on both sides, so "bitter" is the match. The other three fix something else about a quarrel: "brief" its length, "public" its audience, and "unresolved" its outcome. A quarrel can be any of the three while both parties stay perfectly civil.

prompt: OSTRACIZE
choices: praise in front of a group
fine on behalf of a group
explanation: To ostracize someone is to shut him out of the company he belonged to, so "exclude from a group" is the match. "Fine on behalf of a group" is also a punishment, but it takes money and leaves the person where he was; "appoint to lead a group" raises him instead; and "praise in front of a group" honors him. All four are things a community can do to one of its own members.

prompt: Farhan set the timer for the rice, went out to help his sister carry a sofa up three flights, and came back half an hour after the timer had rung to find the burner still lit and the grains at the bottom of the pot -------.
explanation: The burner was still lit half an hour past the time the rice needed, so the grains lying against the hot metal are "burned." "Cold" would need the heat to have stopped, and the sentence says it had not; "undercooked" would need less cooking than the rice got rather than more; and "unsalted" reports what went into the pot at the start, which the extra half hour could not change either way.

prompt: Bao got the date, the address, and a hand-drawn map onto one side of a single sheet, but only by shrinking the type twice and running the map into the margin, so the finished poster looked -------.
explanation: Three things forced onto one side of one sheet, with the type shrunk twice and the map pushed into the margin, is a page carrying more than it has room for: "cluttered." "Blank" is refused by the three things the sentence puts on it; "faded" would report the state of the ink, which the sentence never raises; and "formal" would describe how the poster is worded rather than how it is packed, and not a word of its wording is given.

prompt: Kofi's grandmother kept one account book for forty years, and on every page the date, the item, and the price stand in the same three narrow columns; whatever else may be said of her bookkeeping, it was -------.
explanation: Forty years of pages laid out in the same three columns is one method held to without variation, which is what "consistent" names. "Incomplete" is refused by the sentence's own list — date, item, and price on every page; "legible" would report how clearly the hand was formed, and what the sentence describes is the arrangement of the columns rather than the writing inside them; and "disputed" would need someone to have challenged the figures, and no second person appears in the sentence at all.

prompt: Six weeks of cold rain kept the crew off the roof, and in August the ladders were still leaning where they had been left, so the job that was to have been done by April was -------.
explanation: The weather stopped the work and the work was never taken up again, so the job stands "unfinished." "Abandoned" is refused by the ladders still leaning where they were left, since a crew that has given up takes its ladders away; "rescheduled" would need someone to have named a new date, and nobody in the sentence names one; and "condemned" would apply to the building rather than to the job, and nothing here says the building was declared unsafe.

prompt: A book from the lending library may be renewed twice and no more; the cap is there to keep one reader's hold on a title from becoming -------.
explanation: Two renewals and no more sets a limit on how long one reader may keep a book, so what the cap prevents is a hold that runs on without end: "indefinite." "Occasional" runs the other way, since a hold that came and went is exactly what a cap on renewals still permits; "hereditary" would have the book pass from one reader to another, which the rule says nothing about; and "customary" would describe a practice the library had fallen into rather than the length of one reader's hold, and it is that length a limit of two renewals measures.

prompt: The instruction to cook the onions 'until they are done' left Priya with nothing she could act on, since done might mean soft, or browned, or nearly dissolved, depending on the dish; the direction was -------.
explanation: A direction that allows three different stopping points has not said which one it means, so it is "imprecise." "Incorrect" would mean the direction said something false, and each of the three readings it allows is a real way to cook an onion; "unnecessary" would mean the step could be dropped, and the onions must still be cooked somehow; and "condescending" would describe the recipe's attitude toward the cook, which the sentence never reports.

prompt: Tomás has opened with the same four chords at every performance for two years, and the regulars at the front can hum the whole set before he plays a note; his playing is expert but -------.
explanation: An audience that can hum the set before it starts already knows what is coming, which is what "predictable" names. "Amateurish" is refused by "expert" in the same clause; "hurried" would report a pace, and the sentence gives no tempo at all; and "quiet" would report volume, which has nothing to do with the sameness the regulars have noticed.

prompt: Every spring the council votes the money to repaint the crosswalks, and every winter the plows take the paint off again; after twenty years the repainting has become less a repair than a -------.
explanation: Twenty years of an act performed on schedule and undone on schedule is something a town does because the season has come round again, which is what "ritual" names. "Hazard" would attach to a crosswalk with no paint on it rather than to the act of painting it; "experiment" would mean the council was testing something, and twenty identical springs are the opposite of a trial; and "concession" would need someone on the other side to be yielding to, and the sentence puts no one there.

prompt: Oduya replies to every message within the hour, and the reply is always the same sentence saying that the message has arrived and that a proper answer will follow; what he is quick at is not answering but -------.
explanation: A sentence reporting that the message has arrived does one thing only — it confirms receipt — and that is "acknowledging." "Apologizing" would need him to express regret, and the sentence he sends expresses none; "delegating" would hand the message on to somebody else, and no one else appears; and "refusing" would send the sender away, while a promise that a proper answer will follow does the reverse.

prompt: The grant bought the department its best microscope but paid for no one to run it, and for two years the instrument stood in a locked room, -------.
explanation: An instrument that nobody is paid to operate does nothing at all, so it stands "idle." "Obsolete" is refused by the sentence's own claim that it is the best microscope the department has; "damaged" would need something to have happened to it, and a locked room is precisely where nothing happens to it; and "borrowed" would put the ownership somewhere else, while the grant bought it outright.

prompt: Zubair put up a sign asking customers not to keep a table for more than an hour, never once enforced it, and has left it hanging by the door for five years; the regulars long ago decided that the notice was -------.
explanation: A rule that is posted and never enforced asks rather than requires, which is what "advisory" names. "Binding" is refused by the five years in which no customer was ever held to it; "temporary" is refused instead by the sign itself, which has hung by the door that whole time; and "insulting" would report an offense taken, and the sentence says nothing about any customer minding.

prompt: The report was ------- about the cause of the outage and ------- about the remedy: it named the failed relay, the minute it failed, and the engineer on duty, and then said only that steps would be taken.
explanation: The colon divides the sentence the way the report divides itself: three named particulars for the cause — "specific" — and one empty phrase for the remedy, which is "evasive." "Cautious . . . detailed" has the halves the wrong way round, thin where the report is full and full where it is thin; "hostile . . . apologetic" describes a temper rather than an amount of information, and no temper is on display in a list of relays and minutes; and "technical . . . lengthy" is fair enough on the first blank but breaks on the second, since a promise that steps would be taken is the shortest thing in the report.

prompt: For forty years Halloway's life of the poet was the only one, and every later writer on the subject quoted it; when his sources were examined in 1998 and half of them turned out to be letters in private hands that no one else had ever been shown, four decades of scholarship became -------.
explanation: If half the evidence sits where nobody else can get at it, nothing resting on that evidence can be checked, and the work built on Halloway is "unverifiable." "Plagiarized" would mean the later writers had taken his work without saying so, and the sentence says they quoted him; "outdated" would make the passage of time the trouble, while the trouble is that the letters cannot be reached at any date; and "irrelevant" would mean the scholarship no longer bore on the poet, and nothing in the sentence has changed what it is about.

prompt: The society's charter gives a member ten days from a decision in which to file an objection, and forbids the officers to publish any decision until sixty days have gone by; a member who wishes to object is therefore obliged to do so before the decision is -------.
explanation: Ten days in which to object, and no publication for sixty, means the window shuts a full fifty days before the decision reaches the membership, so the objection has to be filed while the member still cannot have learned what was decided — before it is "known." "Final" runs against the charter's own order, since the ten days begin from a decision already taken; "contested" turns the sentence back on itself, because filing the objection is what contesting the decision consists of; and "enforced" concerns what is done with a decision afterward, which neither of the charter's two rules touches.

prompt: The survey asked residents whether they would like better transit and reported that 94 percent would; because no one was asked what better transit might cost or replace, the 94 percent tells us less about the town than about the question's -------.
explanation: A question that offers a benefit and names no price is built so that almost anyone can agree with it, so what the 94 percent reflects is the way the question was put: its "phrasing." "Timing" would make the moment of asking the trouble, and the sentence gives no date; "audience" would put the fault in who was asked, while residents are exactly the people whose opinion was wanted and the omission described sits inside the question itself; and "sponsor" would need some interested party behind the survey, and none appears.

prompt: Bergen's expedition notebooks give the weather for every day of the crossing, the condition of the dogs, and the exact weight of the rations, and dispose of the two deaths in a single line each; across four hundred pages that proportion never varies, and the reticence comes to look less like oversight than -------.
explanation: A proportion held to for four hundred pages is a rule its writer is keeping rather than something he failed to notice, and keeping to such a rule is "discipline." "Custom" would make the practice one that expedition diaries share, and the sentence sets no other notebook beside Bergen's; "modesty" would concern how he writes about himself, while the two lines he grudges are about other men; and "superstition" would need him to hold some belief about naming a death, and the sentence reports no belief of any kind.
